questions.prompt: Reading: Character, Setting, and Problem (3 points) Stanley Lambchop was a cheerful boy who lived with his parents and his younger brother Arthur. keyConcepts: 🔍 How to Do It Read both texts: Read the story passage and the informational text carefully. Look for similarities: What topic or ideas do both texts share? Spot the differences: How does the story tell it differently from the informational text? 🧠 Think about this Today you’ll read about how real mail travels. What do you think will be the same and different between Stanley’s trip and how real mail is sent? 📓 Your thoughts

📌 Examples pre- + view = preview — prefix pre- means before pre- + heat = preheat — heat before you cook pre- + pay = prepay — pay before you use 🧩 Practice: Find the Base Word! pre- + test = pre- + school = pre- + heat = pre- + pay = Check My Answers 🌱 All correct!
📌 Let's try it together: “insurance”

🔍 What Does “Revise” Mean? Revise means to re-see your writing. You’re not fixing spelling yet — you’re making your ideas stronger and clearer. Ask yourself: 📌 Does my story make sense from beginning to end? 📌 Did I include enough details so my reader can picture what happened? 📌 Does it sound like me telling the story? 📌 Is there a part that’s confusing or needs more detail? 📌 Does each sentence add something important to my story?

👀 Sam’s Revision: Before & After Before (Draft + Craft) I was playing in the yard when I saw Bingo run out the gate. I ran after him. He was fast. I was scared he would get lost. I finally caught him at the park. After (Revised) I was playing in the yard when I saw the gate swing open. Bingo shot out like a rocket and took off down the sidewalk! I ran after him, my heart pounding so loud I could hear it in my ears. He was way too fast. What if he got lost and never came home? I finally spotted him at the park, rolling in the mud with the biggest smile on his face.

🔍 Revise vs. Edit — What’s the Difference? Revise = Big Changes Add details, move sentences around, make ideas clearer. (You did this yesterday!) Edit = Small Fixes Fix spelling, capitals, punctuation, and grammar. (Today’s job!)

📋 Today’s Tool: Editing Checklist ☐ Every sentence starts with a capital letter . ☐ Every sentence ends with the right punctuation (. ? !) ☐ Proper nouns are capitalized (names, places, titles). ☐ I checked my spelling — especially vowel teams (ai/ay, oa/ow). ☐ My beginning hooks the reader and starts the story. ☐ My ending wraps up the story and feels finished.

👀 Sam’s Editing: Before & After Before (needs editing) i was playing in the yard when i saw the gate swing open. bingo shot out like a rocket and took off down the sidewalk! i ran after him my heart pounding so loud I could hear it in my ears After (edited) I was playing in the yard when I saw the gate swing open. B ingo shot out like a rocket and took off down the sidewalk! I ran after him , my heart pounding so loud I could hear it in my ears .

keyConcepts: 🔍 How to Do It Read both texts: Read the story passage and the informational text carefully. Look for similarities: What topic or ideas do both texts share? Spot the differences: How does the story tell it differently from the informational text? 🧠 Think about this Today you’ll compare the story’s Famous Museum with real museums. What do you already know about museums? How might a real museum be different from the one in the story? 📓 Your thoughts

📌 Examples pre- + view = preview — see before 🧩 Practice: Find the Base Word! You should ____________ the oven before baking cookies. We got to ____________ the movie before it came out. You can ____________ for your lunch so you don’t have to bring money. My little sister goes to ____________ because she is only four. Check My Answers 🌱 All correct!

📋 Final Draft Tips 📌 Write your story neatly from the beginning — this is your publish copy! 📌 Include all the improvements from revising and editing. 📌 Make sure your story has a clear beginning, middle, and end . 📌 Read it one more time when you’re done. Does it sound like you telling the story?

👀 Sam’s Final Draft It was a sunny Saturday morning, and I was playing fetch with Bingo in the backyard. Then I saw something that made my stomach drop — the gate was wide open. Bingo shot out like a rocket and took off down the sidewalk! I ran after him, my heart pounding so loud I could hear it in my ears. He was way too fast. “Bingo, come back!” I yelled, but he just kept running. What if he got lost and never came home? I followed him all the way to Miller Park. When I finally found him, he was rolling in the mud with the biggest smile on his face. I clipped on his leash with shaking hands and hugged him, mud and all. That was the day I learned to always double-check the gate. And Bingo? He got the longest bath of his life. Notice: Sam’s final draft has all his revisions and edits included. It’s clean, clear, and ready to share! 📝 Now you try. Write your clean final draft below. Include all your revisions and edits. This is the version you’ll publish tomorrow! How did reading the real-world text change the way you thought about the story? 🧠 Think about this Flat Stanley is fiction, but it touches on real topics like mailing packages, visiting museums, and being different. 📌 Remember The prefix pre- means before . When you add pre- to a word, it changes the meaning to "before [that word]." 🎲 Dice Roll Challenge! Roll the dice and explain the pre- word you land on. What does the prefix do to the meaning? ⚀ 🎲 Roll the Dice! 0/6 words rolled

📮 What Does “Publish” Mean? When real authors finish writing, they publish — they share their work with readers! Today, YOU are the author. Publishing means writing your very best final copy and sharing it so others can read and enjoy it. 📋 Publish-Ready Checklist ☐ My story has a clear beginning, middle, and end . ☐ I wrote from my point of view (using “I” and “me”). ☐ I included specific details so my reader can picture what happened. ☐ I shared how I felt during the moment. ☐ All proper nouns are capitalized and punctuation is correct . ☐ My story is neat and easy to read .

👀 Sam’s Published Story It was a sunny Saturday morning, and I was playing fetch with Bingo in the backyard. Then I saw something that made my stomach drop — the gate was wide open. Bingo shot out like a rocket and took off down the sidewalk! I ran after him, my heart pounding so loud I could hear it in my ears. He was way too fast. “Bingo, come back!” I yelled, but he just kept running. What if he got lost and never came home? I followed him all the way to Miller Park. When I finally found him, he was rolling in the mud with the biggest smile on his face. I clipped on his leash with shaking hands and hugged him, mud and all. That was the day I learned to always double-check the gate. And Bingo? He got the longest bath of his life.

Think about your writing process. 📓 What is one thing you learned about writing that you want to remember? 🎉📮✨ Congratulations, Published Author! keyConcepts: 📌 Skill Pacing — slow down for wonder, speed up for action Read with wonder and careful pacing. 📌 The Rule An apostrophe has two jobs. (1) In a contraction, it replaces a missing letter: can't = can + not. (2) In a possessive, it shows ownership: Aslan's mane = the mane belonging to Aslan. It's Aslan's roar that shakes the Witch's walls.

📌 The Pattern The schwa is the most common vowel sound in English. It sounds like 'uh' and can be spelled with any vowel: a, e, i, o, or u. Example: about — the a sounds like 'uh.' 📌 The Rule When writing dialogue: (1) Put quotation marks around the exact words spoken. (2) The first word of speech gets a capital letter. keyConcepts: 📌 Let's try it together: “courageous”

📌 The Rule Spiral review: A complete sentence needs a subject and a verb and expresses a complete thought. Complex sentences add a dependent clause with a connecting word (when, because, although, if). Compound sentences join two complete thoughts with a comma + conjunction (and, but, so, or). Although he was small, Despereaux refused to give up his quest.

📌 The Pattern When you see a long word, break it into parts: prefix + base + suffix. Example: un + courage + ous = uncourageous. Use what you know about each part to read and spell the whole word. 🎮 Sort these words into the correct spelling pattern group. courageous fearless rebuild unafraid transform hopeful interact careless Has a prefix
🌟 Reading–Writing–Meaning Connection Compare/contrast language shows how two texts connect.

keyConcepts: 📌 Let's try it together: “integrity”

📌 The Rule Final editing checklist: (1) Every sentence begins with a capital letter. (2) Proper nouns (names, titles, places) are always capitalized. (3) Apostrophes in contractions and possessives are correct. (4) Commas before and/but/so joining complete thoughts. (5) Dialogue punctuation is correct. (6) Consistent verb tense throughout. Although Edmund made a terrible mistake, his courage and honesty at the end of the story showed that he had changed.

📌 The Pattern Year-end review: when you see an unfamiliar word, break it apart. Ask: Is there a prefix? A base word I recognize? A suffix? Use all three to figure out the meaning. Then check your spelling by thinking about the syllable type of each part. 🎮 Sort these words into the correct spelling pattern group. honesty courageous unafraid rebuild fearless transform perseverance respectful Has a prefix
🌟 Reading–Writing–Meaning Connection Speaking and writing with a clear, confident voice.

View the Course Syllabus
Course Overview

Grade 3 Language Arts develops independent reading, analytical thinking, written expression, vocabulary, grammar, speaking, and listening. Students read literature and informational texts, discuss central ideas and author choices, use text evidence, and revise writing using standard English conventions.

Core Course Areas
• Literature and informational reading
• What Good Readers Do
• Vocabulary and context clues
• Morphology, spelling, and word analysis
• Grammar and conventions
• RWM sentence study
• Weekly fluency practice
• Narrative, opinion, and expository writing
• Research and oral presentation
• Portfolio and final reflection
A Typical ELA Learning Pathway
Welcome and Roadmap Learn the goal, needed materials, and order of the lesson.
Language and Word Study Practice grammar, spelling, morphology, vocabulary, or sentence study.
Reading Focus Read with a purpose and use a Good Reader habit.
Guided Practice Follow teacher modeling, examples, and supported practice.
Writing Connection Apply reading, vocabulary, grammar, or sentence skills in writing.
Self-Check and Turn-In Review, revise, and submit the required work.
How Work Is Reviewed
Area What Strong Work Shows
Reading Understanding The response accurately explains the text and uses relevant details.
Text Evidence Ideas are supported with details, examples, or quotations when assigned.
Writing The writing fits its purpose, is organized, and includes clear details.
Language and Conventions Grammar, punctuation, capitalization, spelling, and vocabulary support meaning.
Revision and Communication The student uses feedback, revises thoughtfully, and communicates clearly.
Fluency and Writing Projects

Fluency: Once per week, students usually listen to a model, read for accuracy, reread for smoothness, reread with expression, and submit a final recording.

Major writing: Larger projects use the writing process—brainstorm, plan, draft, revise, edit, and publish. Some weeks may focus more heavily on the writing project.
